title: Getting the tax wrong

predict.q: The true external cost is 20 per unit. The government sets a tax per unit equal to its estimate. It overestimates the external cost and sets a tax of 30. What happens?

options.s: Output falls to the social optimum; the extra tax does no harm
options.fb: Output now falls to 25, below Q* = 30. Units 25–30 were worth more to society than they cost, and they are lost.

options.s: Output falls below the social optimum, and a new welfare loss (deadweight loss) appears
options.fb: Output falls to 25, below Q* = 30: a new welfare loss of 25 appears, on the other side of Q*.

options.s: Output stays at the market level, because firms pass the tax on to consumers
options.fb: The tax raises firms' costs, so supply shifts up and output falls; passing on part of the tax does not stop that.

options.s: The welfare loss becomes bigger than with no tax at all
options.fb: The new loss (25) is smaller than the loss with no tax (100). Overcorrecting is costly, but here less so than doing nothing.

task: Move the tax slider from 0 to 40 and watch output and the shaded triangle.

target.do: Set the tax to 30, then press Check.

takeaway: The tax corrects the market only if it matches the true external cost, so measurement matters. When the tax equals the true MEC, MSB = MSC at the chosen output, and the deadweight loss disappears.
